title: Organisations and projects, simply explained
description: Understand how to organise several locations, switch workspaces, and keep each location's recordings in the right place.

editorialStyle.tone: A short, high-level introduction for a first-time listener. Explain why the topic matters, build one mental model, and suggest one next action. Sound like two colleagues, not a narrated manual.
editorialStyle.scope: Aim for four to five minutes and roughly 500-550 spoken words. Use one fictional example and four short chapters. Leave identifiers, form limits, configuration, migration mechanics, and troubleshooting checklists in the linked guide. Keep essential caveats as practical consequences.
editorialStyle.humour: Optional: one or two brief, relevant light moments are enough. Prefer a relatable analogy over a separate joke. Never pad the overview with banter.
editorialStyle.reactions: Use occasional short, natural responses followed by a real question. Avoid repetitive praise, canned agreement, and filler.
editorialStyle.laughter: Optional: at most one light spoken reaction. Never insert [laughs], SSML, or repeated ha-ha strings. A spoken reaction is not a guarantee of genuine laughter from the current speech engine.
editorialStyle.intonation: Write real questions with question marks, use contractions, alternate short and longer sentences, and make contrasts explicit. Let punctuation and sentence rhythm suggest curiosity and emphasis.
editorialStyle.guardrails: Keep technical claims source-backed. Never imply planned access controls are live or omit essential safety and compatibility caveats. Explain their practical consequence without narrating the implementation.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Imagine your team monitors a warehouse and a shop. Both use the same platform, but you don't want their daily work mixed together. How do organisations and projects help? Let's explain the big picture with that fictional example.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The organisation is the shared home for the business: its ownership, members, and billing. Inside it, projects keep operational resources separate. Our company could use one project for the warehouse and another for the shop.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: So we can organise the work around real locations, rather than put everything in one big pile. Does that mean a different login for every project?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: No extra collection of passwords. One user identity can work across several organisations. Projects don't require separate accounts. The important distinction is between where resources belong and what you're currently working on.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: That's where the word workspace comes in, isn't it? We've already got an organisation and a project. Please tell me there isn't a third box to create.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: There isn't. Workspace just means the organisation and project you've selected together. Think of the organisation as the company, the project as one location's work, and the workspace as the place you're looking at right now.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Company, location, current view. That feels manageable. But choosing the warehouse doesn't automatically give me permission to see all its cameras?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Right. Selection isn't permission, and membership alone doesn't grant access either. Hub still uses its existing access controls. The guide separates what's available today from the newer role-assignment design, so administrators shouldn't treat that design as a live access-management feature.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Let's follow a normal morning. I'm checking the warehouse, then I switch to the shop. What actually changes?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Your working view changes to the selected organisation and project. The warehouse cameras and recordings stay in the warehouse project. Switching is navigation, not a moving service.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Good. No tiny removal van for the cameras. What if a warehouse recording is still being processed when I switch?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Its results still belong with the warehouse recording. Background processing follows the source, not your next click. And on an existing installation, older recordings remain available in their owner's default project without requiring a data migration first.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: So an empty new project doesn't mean the old recordings disappeared. I should check which workspace I'm looking at.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Exactly. A new project is a separate place for work, not a copy of the old one. Check your selected workspace and access before assuming anything has gone missing.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Before we go, what's the simplest way to remember all this?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: The organisation is the shared home. Projects separate operational work inside it. Your workspace is the organisation and project you're using now. Switching changes your view, not ownership or permissions.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Identify the organisation and project your team should use, then check the current access controls with your administrator. If the workspace controls aren't visible, the guide explains how to enable them. It also has the exact setup steps when you're ready.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Start with the right workspace; keep the detailed guide nearby. That's the overview.
